title: Paleoinspired Vision: From Exploring Colour Vision Evolution to Inspiring Camera Design
claim: One framework traces a lineage's evolutionary trajectory and tests several downstream hypotheses and applications across distinct environments.
layout: 5 sections, left-to-right; phylogeny timeline on left, hypothesis panels right
description: A wide figure with a long arrow along the top marked 518, 210 and 65 Mya. On the left, a phylogenetic tree runs from extinct species (Tujiaaspis, Xiushanosteus, Juramaia, Purgatorius) to modern animals (lamprey, birds, lizards, turtles, whales, rodents, monkeys, humans). Below it, yellow labels (Vertebrates, Mammals, Primates) sit over cone-opsin icons and gene strings such as LWS/SWS1/SWS2/RH2. Green arrows link them, with orange Gene Loss and Gene Duplication tags, and the crossed-out genes show loss. On the right, three boxed panels separated by dashed blue lines cover Color Blindness (fruit recognition, dim-light advantage), Deep Sea Creature (squirrelfish, blueshift, multiple rod opsins) and Hypothetical Martian Vision (Mars photo, spectral curves). Section tags (Sec 4.1 to Sec 5) sit at the bottom. The eye goes first to the colorful animal photos.
caption: Our framework reconstructs the 518-million-year evolutionary trajectory of color vision across the vertebrate-to-primate lineage and evaluates corresponding explanatory hypotheses. This includes the transition from ancestral tetrachromacy through mammalian gene loss (dichromatic regression) to primate gene duplication (trichromatic progression). Furthermore, the framework quantifies the dim-light advantage hypothesis, deep-sea opsin blueshifts, and predictive visual adaptations and sensor designs for novel environments, such as the Martian landscape.
abstract: The evolution of colour vision is captivating, as it reveals the adaptive strategies of extinct species while simultaneously inspiring innovations in modern imaging technology. In this study, we present a simplified model of visual transduction in the retina, introducing a novel opsin layer. We quantify evolutionary pressures by measuring machine vision recognition accuracy on colour images shaped by specific opsins. Building on this, we develop an evolutionary conservation optimisation algorithm to reconstruct the spectral sensitivity of opsins, enabling mutation-driven adaptations to more effectively spot fruits or predators. This model condenses millions of years of evolution into seconds using GPU, providing an experimental framework to test long-standing hypotheses in evolutionary biology, such as vision of early mammals, primate trichromacy from gene duplication, retention of colour blindness, blue-shift of fish rod and multiple rod opsins with bioluminescence. Beyond validating existing paleontological hypotheses, our model further enables speculative explorations of hypothetical species, such as organisms with visual systems adapted to Martian conditions. These constitute our contributions to AI for life science and neuroscience. Besides, the principles derived from these biological studies can translate into practical engineering solutions. In practice, our findings suggest a minimalist yet effective approach to task-specific camera filter design, optimising the spectral response function to meet application-driven demands. Code repository: https://github.com/luyijie-research/PaleVision.
